warmup.q: The payments program saves a new payment in PostgreSQL and then sends a PaymentAuthorized message to Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages for other programs to read. Which change makes the message reach Kafka if, and only if, the payment is saved?
options: Wrap the insert and the send in one of Kafka's own transactions, which group several Kafka writes into one
Send the message first, then insert the payment, and retry the send until it works
Insert an event row into a second table in the same database transaction as the payment, and let Debezium publish it from the database's log
Turn on Kafka's idempotent producer, which drops repeated sends
warmup.why: The event row makes it one write to one database: the payment and its event are saved together or not at all, and Debezium publishes only saved (committed) rows, in commit order. That's the outbox. A Kafka transaction covers Kafka writes only, never the database, and the proposal that would let Kafka join a database's transaction (KIP-939) hasn't shipped. Sending first announces payments that may never be saved, and after a crash a retry can't tell which half happened. The idempotent producer removes repeats caused by its own retries; it doesn't tie the send to the database.

sections.h: Kafka Connect: a ready-made follower for every table
sections.html:
The last lesson ended with a follower we wrote ourselves. It peeked at a slot (PostgreSQL's record of how far one reader has read its log), applied each committed transaction, kept a bookmark and confirmed it. That works for one table and one index. The payments company has forty tables. Their changes should feed a search index, a cache and a data lake, plus three other teams' programs. (A cache is a quick copy kept in memory; a data lake is cheap files in Amazon's S3 storage, kept for big reports.) Forty tables times six readers is a lot of followers to write by hand.

Kafka is the natural middle. It's a program that keeps named logs of messages, called topics, and any number of programs can read a topic at their own pace, each keeping its own place. That's what the Messaging and logs track built. So each table's changes go into one topic, and every reader follows the topic instead of the database. What's left is the program in the middle. It has to batch changes, retry after errors, keep a bookmark that survives a crash, run several copies at once, and turn records into bytes and back.

Kafka Connect is that program, written once. It comes with Kafka, and you configure it instead of coding it. Its parts:

  • A worker is one running copy of the Connect program. Workers that share the same group.id form a Connect cluster and split the work between them. Consumers, the programs that read a topic, share a topic the same way in Consumer groups and rebalancing. When a worker dies, the others take over its work.
  • A connector is one configured copy job: a plug-in plus its settings. You create one by sending a web request (a POST) to Connect's REST API, the web addresses on port 8083 where it takes commands. A source connector reads an outside system and writes to Kafka; a sink connector reads Kafka and writes out.
  • A task does the copying. A connector splits its job into up to tasks.max tasks, and the cluster spreads them over its workers.
  • A converter turns Connect's records into the bytes stored in Kafka and back. JsonConverter writes JSON, StringConverter writes plain text, and a registry-aware Avro converter writes a compact binary form that the next section explains.
  • A transform, short for single message transform (SMT), changes each record on the way: it renames a field, hides a card number, or sends the record to another topic.

Connect keeps its own state in three Kafka topics: connect-configs for the connectors' settings, connect-status for which task runs where, and connect-offsets for each source connector's bookmark. All three are compacted. Kafka keeps only the latest message for each key, a label each message can carry, the way a new note on a notice board replaces the old one with the same title (Partitions and segments on disk: retention and compaction). Kafka 4.4 adds connect-internal-topics.sh (KIP-1209), so you can create those topics yourself, with the settings you choose.

The source connector that matters here is Debezium 3.7, the free program from the last lesson that reads databases' logs. Its PostgreSQL connector is the last lesson's follower, built for real use. It creates a slot, copies the tables first, then reads the slot in pgoutput, PostgreSQL's compact change format. Each row change becomes a change event with four parts. before and after are the row before and after the change. op says what happened: c for create, u update, d delete, or r for a row read during the first copy. source says where it came from: the LSN (the change's position in the write-ahead log, or WAL), the transaction number and the table.

Each table's events go to their own topic, <prefix>.public.payment, and each event's key is the row's primary key, the column that names the row. Kafka splits a topic into partitions, separate logs that can live on different machines, and keeps order only inside each one. Messages with the same key always land in the same partition. So each row's changes stay in order.

The LSN that Debezium has reached is its bookmark, stored in connect-offsets. Connect saves it about once a minute (offset.flush.interval.ms, 60 s by default), and Debezium then confirms that LSN to the slot. So the last lesson's warnings carry over: some changes arrive twice, and a stopped connector's slot keeps WAL. The figure shows the whole cluster. Next, we'll look at what all six readers now depend on.

sections.h: Renaming a column breaks readers you never met
sections.html:
Now the payments table has six readers, and that changes what a table is. Debezium's events carry the table's columns, so the columns are now something six teams' programs read. One morning, the payment team renames amount to amount_minor, because a new currency counts in thousandths, not hundredths. They make the change in the database. Debezium follows it, and its events now carry amount_minor. The ledger, the program that keeps every account's balance, looks for amount, finds nothing, and records 0.00. Nobody gets an error.

Undoing the rename doesn't clean up, either. The events in the new shape stay in the topic until Kafka's retention, the time it keeps messages, runs out, and anyone who rereads the topic meets both shapes. That's the spreadsheet from the opening, with money in it.

Kafka can't stop this, because a Kafka server stores each message as bytes and never looks inside (The log: Kafka's one big idea). The Encoding track's lesson Schemas that evolve: Protobuf, Avro and compatibility built the two pieces that can. The first is a schema: the written-down shape of a record, with its field names, their types, and a default for each field that may be missing. Think of a printed form with named boxes. The second is a schema registry, a small web service that stores every version of each schema and gives each one a number. It checks every new version against the old ones before anyone writes with it. Here is how the two sit in Kafka.

The usual format is Avro, a compact binary format that leaves field names out of each record, because the schema already has them. A program that writes to Kafka is a producer, and its serializer turns each record into bytes. A registry-aware serializer first registers the record's schema under a subject, <topic>-value by default, and gets back a number, the schema id. (Confluent's Avro, Protobuf and JSON Schema serializers work this way, and so does Connect's Avro converter for Debezium's events.) Then it writes 5 bytes in front of the data: a magic byte 0, which marks the format, and the 4-byte id.

On the other side, a consumer, a program that reads from Kafka, has a schema of its own: the shape its code expects, called the reader's schema. Its deserializer, which turns bytes back into a record, reads the id, fetches the writer's schema once and keeps it, then matches the two by field name with Avro's rules. A field the writer has and the reader doesn't is skipped. A field the reader has and the writer doesn't takes the reader's default. A missing field with no default makes the read fail. In Java, and then in Kotlin, where the same three calls lose new and gain val:

Java
// the consumer's side: the writer's schema comes by id, the reader's schema is the consumer's own
Schema writer = registry.schemaById(schemaIdFromTheFirst5Bytes);
var reader = new GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord>(writer, myPaymentSchema);
GenericRecord payment = reader.read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(avroBytes, null));
Kotlin
// the consumer's side: the writer's schema comes by id, the reader's schema is the consumer's own
val writer: Schema = registry.schemaById(schemaIdFromTheFirst5Bytes)
val reader = GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord>(writer, myPaymentSchema)
val payment: GenericRecord = reader.read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(avroBytes, null))

(registry.schemaById stands for what the registry-aware deserializer does for you.)

With a registry in front of the topic, the rename fails early and loudly. The converter can't register a version that old records can't be read with, so the connector's task stops with an error, instead of publishing records the ledger can't read. A stopped connector is still trouble, but it's trouble with an alarm, and the last lesson said what to watch on the database while it waits. Next, we'll see how the registry decides which changes to refuse.

try.title: Read one payment with three reader schemas
steps: Run AvroEvolutionDemo from the labs folder (command below). It needs no Kafka and no registry, only Avro's own library inside the JVM, the program that runs Java and Kotlin code.

It writes a payment with schema v1, then reads the same bytes with three reader schemas: v1, v2 (which adds currency, with a default) and v3 (which adds merchantId, with none). Predict which reads fail before it prints.

No broker, no registry. */ public class AvroEvolutionDemo { static final String V1 = """ {"type": "record", "name": "Payment", "fields": [ {"name": "id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "account", "type": "string"}, {"name": "amount", "type": "long"}]}"""; static final String V2 = """ {"type": "record", "name": "Payment", "fields": [ {"name": "id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "account", "type": "string"}, {"name": "amount", "type": "long"}, {"name": "currency", "type": "string", "default": "EUR"}]}"""; sections.h: Who upgrades first decides what the registry refuses
sections.html:
Before it accepts a new version, the registry runs that same reader rule, in the direction the subject's compatibility mode names. There are three directions. BACKWARD, the default, means a reader with the new schema can read data written with the latest one. So consumers can move to the new schema first, while producers still write the old one. FORWARD means readers on the latest schema can read data written with the new one, so producers can move first. FULL means both, so the order is free.

Each mode has a _TRANSITIVE twin that checks against every version ever registered, not only the latest. A compacted topic needs it, because its version 1 records may never be deleted.

So the question that picks the mode for a topic is: who changes first?

  • Events your own team designs, such as the topic payments-value. Your team can update the readers before the writers, so BACKWARD fits, or BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE if the topic is compacted.
  • CDC topics, which Debezium fills from a table's changes (CDC is change data capture). Here the database changes first: a change to the table is the producer's change, and every consumer meets the new shape at once. That calls for FORWARD or FULL, because old consumers must read new records.

Under FORWARD, some table changes pass and some don't. A nullable column may be empty (NULL), so dropping one passes: old readers fill it with null. A NOT NULL column must always have a value, so dropping or renaming one is refused. Renaming a nullable column passes, and old consumers quietly read null from then on. The registry checks shapes, not meaning, as the Encoding track warned.

When the registry refuses a version, the tempting fix is to set the subject's mode to NONE, which turns the check off. The version goes in, and the failure moves to a consumer, later, or to a replay next month. Make the change compatible instead: give the new field a default, or rename in two steps, as the worked example does. Then make the registry the only way in:

  • Set auto.register.schemas=false on production producers, and register schemas from CI after review. CI (continuous integration) is the automatic build that runs on every change to the code. Without this setting, any new version of a producer registers whatever its code happens to say.
  • In CI, POST the candidate schema to /compatibility/subjects/<subject>/versions/latest and fail the build if the answer is false.
  • A refused registration comes back as HTTP 409, the web's "conflict" answer, with error code 40901 and a reason such as READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE.

Back at the office, the registry is the clerk who approves each new version of a printed form. Under BACKWARD, the clerk's rule is that a person holding the new form must still be able to read every old one in the filing cabinet. A new box is fine, as long as the form says what to assume when it's empty. The stepper shows one check under the default mode, and the Try it runs the same checks against a real registry. Then we'll go back to the payment that started all this, and give its readers an event designed for them.

try.title: Ask a real registry
steps: From the labs folder, start the Kafka broker with Schema Registry: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml --profile schemas up -d --wait. The registry takes about a minute the first time.
Run RegistryDemo (command below). Over the registry's REST API, it reads the global mode, registers v1, checks and registers v2, then checks v3 and tries to register it.
Predict the HTTP status of the last POST before you run it.

sections.h: The outbox: an event you designed, saved in the same transaction
sections.html:
Back to the payment. The payments program authorizes a payment, asking the bank to set the money aside, and inserts its row into PostgreSQL. Now it must tell the ledger, with an event called PaymentAuthorized. The last lesson gives us two ways to do it, and both fall short.

A producer.send after the insert is a dual write, two writes to two systems with nothing tying them together. A crash between the two loses the event, and sending first announces a payment that may never be saved. Kafka has transactions of its own, but they group Kafka writes only and can't include the database (Transactions and exactly-once). KIP-939, a proposal to let Kafka join two-phase commit (the protocol that makes several systems commit together), still hasn't shipped. Plain CDC on the payment table avoids the dual write, but it publishes rows in the table's own shape, the problem of the last two sections. And an UPDATE of status says nothing about why it happened. Was the payment captured, or did someone correct a mistake?

The transactional outbox fixes both. The program inserts the payment row and an event row into a table called outbox, in the same database transaction, so both are saved or neither is. The outbox row has its own schema, designed for its readers, and it changes only when you decide. It's still two writes, but both go to one database in one transaction, the one place where all-or-nothing is cheap. Debezium then captures only the outbox table. It works like an old carbon-copy form: the shop writes the sale and the courier's note on one sheet, so one can't exist without the other.

A simple poller could move the rows instead. Every second, it runs SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE sent = false, publishes what it finds and marks it sent. That costs a query every second on the payments database and up to a second of delay. It also hides an ordering trap. Each new row gets the next id when it's inserted, but it becomes visible only when its transaction commits. So a poller that reads by id can skip a row whose transaction committed late. Reading the WAL has no such gap, because decoding hands out transactions in commit order.

Each outbox row says what the event is about in two columns: aggregatetype, the kind of thing (payment), and aggregateid, which one (here the account, acct-17). Debezium's outbox event router is a transform that turns each outbox insert into a Kafka record. The topic is outbox.event.<aggregatetype>, the key is aggregateid, the value is the payload, and the event's id goes in a header named id, a label that travels with the message. With the account as aggregateid, each account's events keep their order in one partition. The costs are extra writes on the payments database and rows to clean up. The router ignores deletes, so the program can delete each outbox row in the same transaction, right after inserting it, and the table stays empty.

Delivery is still at-least-once. Connect saves the LSN about once a minute, and after a crash in between, Debezium sends the events since the last save again, with the same ids. So consumers dedupe. They keep the ids of the events they have applied and drop repeats, in the same transaction as their own work (Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees).

Publish what you meant, not what your table looks like. Write it in the same transaction.

The outbox keeps the table as the truth, and the events as its announcements. Next, we'll ask what changes if you turn that around.

video.title: Save it and say it, together: the transactional outbox

opening:
Picture a shared spreadsheet that a whole office uses. One sheet lists the sales, and three other sheets pull numbers from its "Amount" column. One morning, someone tidies up and renames the column to "Amount (cents)". Their own sheet looks fine. The other three now show zero for every sale, and nobody is told.

It's an easy mistake to make. A column name feels like your own business: it's your sheet, and the change took a second. But other people built on it, and they can't see you change it.

In Two systems, one truth: dual writes and change data capture, a search index followed the payments database's log, through a follower we wrote by hand. Now six programs want the same changes, and every one of them will read our column names. In this lesson, we'll hand the follower to Kafka Connect and Debezium and put a gatekeeper in front of every change of shape. Then we'll publish events we design on purpose, with the outbox. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a spreadsheet column renamed in a second, and three sheets that went quietly wrong. Our table's columns became that column the moment six programs read its changes. A registry now refuses the change that would break them, and the outbox gives them events we designed, saved with the payment.

In any code you can read, look for a database write followed straight away by a message sent somewhere else: a save and then a send. Each pair is a dual write, and an outbox row is the fix.

Next, we'll turn the outbox around, and ask what happens when the events themselves are the truth and the tables are only copies.

compare.title: The outbox write in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: try (Connection db = dataSource.getConnection()) { db.setAutoCommit(false); // one local transaction for both rows try (var payment = db.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO payment (id, account, amount, status) VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'AUTHORIZED')"); var event = db.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregatetype, aggregateid, type, payload) " + "VALUES (?, 'payment', ?, 'PaymentAuthorized', ?::jsonb)")) { payment.setString(1, paymentId); payment.setString(2, account); payment.setLong(3, cents); payment.executeUpdate(); event.setObject(1, UUID.randomUUID()); // the event id consumers dedupe on event.setString(2, account); // becomes the Kafka key: per-account order event.setString(3, "{\"paymentId\": \"" + paymentId + "\", \"amount\": " + cents + "}"); event.executeUpdate(); } db.commit(); // both rows, or neither }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: dataSource.connection.use { db -> db.autoCommit = false // one local transaction for both rows db.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO payment (id, account, amount, status) VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'AUTHORIZED')").use { it.setString(1, paymentId); it.setString(2, account); it.setLong(3, cents) it.executeUpdate() } db.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregatetype, aggregateid, type, payload) " + "VALUES (?, 'payment', ?, 'PaymentAuthorized', ?::jsonb)").use { it.setObject(1, UUID.randomUUID()) // the event id consumers dedupe on it.setString(2, account) // becomes the Kafka key: per-account order it.setString(3, """{"paymentId": "$paymentId", "amount": $cents}""") it.executeUpdate() } db.commit() // both rows, or neither }

compare.note: The same JDBC calls and the same rule in both languages: both inserts on one connection, auto-commit off, one commit(). (JDBC is Java's standard way to talk to a database.) Java closes the statements with try-with-resources; Kotlin uses use, and its raw string builds the JSON payload without escapes. Neither touches Kafka: the program's only write is to its database, and Debezium publishes the event once the commit is in the WAL. If executeUpdate throws, the connection closes without a commit, PostgreSQL rolls back, and neither row exists.

steps.say: A rename can't happen in one step. Under BACKWARD, a reader with amountMinor and no default can't read old records, and old readers would lose amount. So first add the new field next to the old one, with a default that means "not set".
steps.code: {"type": "record", "name": "Payment", "fields": [ {"name": "id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "account", "type": "string"}, {"name": "amount", "type": "long"}, {"name": "amountMinor", "type": "long", "default": -1}]}

steps.say: Check it against the registry before anything is deployed. In CI, post the candidate to the compatibility endpoint and fail the build on false.
steps.code: curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json' \ --data @payment-v2.json localhost:8081/compatibility/subjects/payments-value/versions/latest # {"is_compatible":true}

steps.say: Deploy the consumers first, as BACKWARD requires. They prefer the new field and fall back to the old one while producers still write -1.
steps.code: long minor = (Long) payment.get("amountMinor"); long cents = minor >= 0 ? minor : (Long) payment.get("amount"); // old records: the default -1

alt.html: val minor = payment.get("amountMinor") as Long val cents = if (minor >= 0) minor else payment.get("amount") as Long // old records: the default -1

steps.say: Then the producers write both fields. When no consumer reads amount any more, and retention has deleted the oldest records that have only amount, register a version without it. BACKWARD accepts the removal, because a new reader skips a field it doesn't know.

lab.title: Build the registry's compatibility check and the outbox relay
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 15 fail. They need no Docker: the schema tests compare your rule with Avro's own SchemaCompatibility, and the outbox tests replay what Debezium did in the Try it.

In CompatibilityChecker.kt, write readProblems(reader, writer). The record names must match. Then, for every reader field: a type the writer's type can't be promoted to (widened safely, like int to long) is a TYPE_MISMATCH, and a field the writer lacks, with no default, is a READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE. canPromote is given.
Write check(mode, candidate, registered): pick the latest version or all of them, as the mode says, and run readProblems in the direction each mode asks for.

In OutboxRelay.java, write route and relay. route handles outbox inserts and first-copy reads only, and sets the topic, key, value and the id and eventType headers. relay collects changes per transaction, routes them at commit, drops rollbacks, and skips commits at or below the stored LSN. Run until all 15 pass.
hints: BACKWARD is readProblems(reader = candidate, writer = latest); FORWARD swaps the two. FULL is both, backward first.
In relay, a LinkedHashMap<Long, List<ChangeEvent>> from transaction id to its changes is enough; the commit entry tells you when to send them.
record.headers().add("id", bytes) adds a header to a ProducerRecord; add id before eventType.

drill.title: The reader rule from memory
drill.prompt: Write, from memory, the rule that decides whether a reader schema can read data written with a writer schema, as a function over lists of fields (names, types, defaults). Then answer: under FORWARD, can you remove currency from the schema if version 2 gave it a default? And under BACKWARD, can you add merchantId without one?

answer.html: fun readProblems(reader: RecordSchema, writer: RecordSchema): List<String> { if (reader.name != writer.name) return listOf("NAME_MISMATCH") val written = writer.fields.associateBy { it.name } return reader.fields.mapNotNull { f -> val w = written[f.name] when { w != null && !canPromote(w.type, f.type) -> "TYPE_MISMATCH: ${f.name}" w == null && !f.hasDefault -> "READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE: ${f.name}" else -> null // same field, or the reader's default fills it; extra writer fields are skipped } } } // FORWARD, remove currency: yes. Old readers (v2) have currency with a default, so they read new records. // BACKWARD, add merchantId with no default: no. A new reader can't fill it from old records: HTTP 409.

alt.html: // record Field(String name, FieldType type, boolean hasDefault) {} // record RecordSchema(String name, List<Field> fields) {} static List<String> readProblems(RecordSchema reader, RecordSchema writer) { if (!reader.name().equals(writer.name())) return List.of("NAME_MISMATCH"); Map<String, Field> written = new HashMap<>(); for (Field f : writer.fields()) written.put(f.name(), f); List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>(); for (Field f : reader.fields()) { Field w = written.get(f.name()); if (w != null && !canPromote(w.type(), f.type())) problems.add("TYPE_MISMATCH: " + f.name()); else if (w == null && !f.hasDefault()) problems.add("READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE: " + f.name()); // otherwise: same field, or the reader's default fills it; extra writer fields are skipped } return problems; } // FORWARD, remove currency: yes. Old readers (v2) have currency with a default, so they read new records. // BACKWARD, add merchantId with no default: no. A new reader can't fill it from old records: HTTP 409.

recap: Kafka Connect runs copy jobs so you don't write them: workers form a cluster, connectors split into tasks, converters turn records into bytes, transforms edit them on the way, and each source's bookmark lives in the connect-offsets topic.

Debezium's PostgreSQL connector is the last lesson's follower for a whole database: a slot, a first copy, then change events (before, after, op, source) on one topic per table, keyed by primary key, with the LSN as its bookmark.

CDC makes a table's columns public. A schema says what shape each record has; a registry-aware serializer puts a 0 byte and a 4-byte schema id in front of each record, and the registry checks every new version before anyone writes with it.

Pick the compatibility mode by who changes first: BACKWARD for events whose readers can update ahead of the writers, FORWARD or FULL for CDC topics, _TRANSITIVE for compacted topics. Keep auto.register.schemas=false in production and check schemas in CI.
The transactional outbox writes the business row and an event row in one database transaction, and Debezium's outbox event router publishes the event, keyed by aggregateid, in commit order.
The limit: it's still at-least-once. After a crash, Debezium repeats the events since the last offset save, with the same ids, so consumers drop repeats by event id.

explain.prompt: A friend's payments program inserts each payment into PostgreSQL and then calls producer.send. Explain what can go wrong, why a retry or a Kafka transaction doesn't fix it, and how the outbox with Debezium does.
explain.answer: They are two writes to two systems with nothing tying them together. A crash after the insert and before the send leaves a payment that no reader hears about; sending first leaves an event for a payment that may never be saved. After a crash the program doesn't know which half happened, so a retry can't put it right. A Kafka transaction only covers Kafka writes and bookmarks, and the two-phase commit proposal, KIP-939, hasn't shipped. With the outbox, the program writes the payment row and an event row in one PostgreSQL transaction, so both exist or neither does. Debezium, running in Kafka Connect, reads the committed rows from the write-ahead log through a replication slot, in commit order, like the last lesson's follower, and the outbox event router publishes each event with the account as its key. Rolled-back transactions never reach the log reader. Debezium can repeat events after a crash, because it saves its WAL position only about once a minute, so readers drop repeats by event id, in the same transaction as their own work.

deeper.html:
The schemas Debezium registers. The Avro converter builds each table's schema from its columns. A NOT NULL column becomes a required field; a nullable one becomes ["null", type] with a null default. That's why, under FORWARD, dropping a nullable column passes and dropping a NOT NULL one doesn't.

Optional fields in your own events. A field that may be missing is a union with null (a field that is either null or a value) and a null default: {"name": "note", "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null}. The default must match the first type in the union, which is why null comes first.

Subject names. The default TopicNameStrategy gives one schema per topic (payments-value). RecordNameStrategy and TopicRecordNameStrategy name the subject after the record type instead, so one topic can carry several event types, each with its own versions. For example, PaymentAuthorized and PaymentCaptured can share one partition and keep their order.

The first copy. When a Debezium connector starts with no stored offset, snapshot.mode=initial reads the captured tables first and sends each existing row as a read event (op = r), slot first and copy second, as the last lesson explained. That's why the Try it's topic started with the row from the WAL peek. For an outbox you usually want only new rows: set snapshot.mode=no_data.

Oracle. Oracle, a large commercial database, keeps its own version of the WAL, called the redo log. Debezium's Oracle connector reads it through a tool called LogMiner by default. The model is the same, a log of committed changes read from a stored position (an SCN instead of an LSN), with more setup: supplemental logging and a LogMiner user.
